tools.description:
Search the web. Routes to a provider adapter automatically (currently enabled providers,
real fallback) unless `provider` is explicitly set. mode controls search depth:
"discover" (snippets only), "answer" (fetches full page content inline for the top
fetch_top_n results, default 10), or "auto" (default -- a deterministic heuristic infers
depth from the query; see AGENT_INSTRUCTIONS). fetch_top_n, if set explicitly, always
overrides mode. min_results, if set, escalates to the next provider when a result set is
thinner than requested. Returns {results: [{link, title, snippet, extracted_text,
content_status, fetch_method, fetch_error, retrieved_at}], provider_used, attempts} --
content_status is one of not_requested/fetched/partially_fetched/fetch_failed/blocked/
unsupported. Check provider_used/attempts to see what actually happened, don't assume.
Content is fetched in provider-returned order, not ranked/reranked -- that judgment stays
with you.
tools.name: search_web

tools.description:
Fetch and extract full page content for one or more URLs (e.g. from search_web's
results, or a URL you already know). SSRF-protected: any URL resolving to localhost, a
private IP range, or a cloud-metadata address is refused, not fetched, and reported with
status "blocked" and a reason. Returns one entry per URL, same order given.
tools.name: fetch_url

tools.description:
Diagnostic status for every internet-search provider this server knows about: whether
it's currently enabled/in the routing chain, its cost class (free/paid), routing priority,
and (if probe=True) a real lightweight live health check. Does NOT select a provider or
perform a search -- purely informational, e.g. to confirm searxng is disabled before
wondering why it never appears in attempts.
tools.name: get_provider_status

tools.description:
Search appropriate scholarly sources and return normalised, deduplicated, ranked research works.

Use when: Exploring a topic, finding publications, or beginning a literature search.
Do NOT use when: You already have a specific DOI/PMID/arXiv ID -- use get_research_work instead, it's more precise and cheaper.
Typically follows: (usually the first tool called for a new topic)
Typically followed by: get_research_work (to reconcile a specific result), resolve_research_access (before requesting content)
Side effects: Calls multiple provider APIs in parallel; no content acquisition happens here.
tools.name: search_research

tools.description:
Retrieve and reconcile one already-known work by identifier.

Use when: You have a DOI, PMID, PMCID, arXiv ID, OpenAlex ID, or Semantic Scholar ID -- or an earlier tool returned one.
Do NOT use when: You're exploring a topic with no specific paper in mind yet -- use search_research first.
Typically follows: search_research (to discover the identifier), or the user supplying one directly
Typically followed by: resolve_research_access, find_related_research
Side effects: None beyond the provider API call(s) needed to reconcile the identifier.
tools.name: get_research_work

tools.description:
Find cited, citing, or semantically related research for a known seed work, where the source provider supports it.

Use when: After identifying a seed paper and you want to explore its citation neighborhood.
Do NOT use when: As the first tool for an unconstrained topic search -- start with search_research instead.
Typically follows: get_research_work or search_research (to get a seed work)
Typically followed by: get_research_work (for selected related works), resolve_research_access (only for the ones you actually need content from)
Side effects: None beyond provider API calls; does not acquire content.
tools.name: find_related_research

tools.description:
Find and reconcile author records.

Use when: Researcher discovery, author disambiguation, or finding works by a specific author.
Do NOT use when: You already have the author's identifier and just want their works -- use search_research with preferred_sources scoped appropriately, or get_research_work per known paper.
Typically follows: (often a first tool, when the request is about a person rather than a topic)
Typically followed by: search_research (constrained to the resolved author), get_research_work
Side effects: None; no content acquisition.
tools.name: search_research_author

tools.description:
Determine whether metadata, abstract, public HTML, public PDF, or another approved content location is available for a work -- WITHOUT fetching it yet.

Use when: Before requesting full content for a specific work.
Do NOT use when: You only need metadata/abstract, which search_research/get_research_work already returned -- don't resolve access you won't use.
Typically follows: get_research_work or a result from search_research
Typically followed by: retrieve_research_content, but ONLY if the resolution actually found a usable location
Side effects: None -- this tool never fetches content, only decides where content might be.
tools.name: resolve_research_access

tools.description:
Retrieve and process content from an already-resolved, approved location.

Use when: After resolve_research_access found a usable location, and you actually need the full text (not just metadata) to answer the request.
Do NOT use when: A metadata record or abstract is already sufficient -- do not acquire content just because you can. Also never for arbitrary unrestricted URLs -- this tool does not accept a bare URL not tied to a resolved work.
Typically follows: resolve_research_access
Typically followed by: get_research_evidence, if you need to cite/verify how the content was obtained
Side effects: Performs a real network fetch (HTTP -> Crawl4AI -> bounded Playwright fallback), SSRF-protected. May be slow for the Playwright tier.
tools.name: retrieve_research_content

tools.description:
Return provider provenance, source identifiers, access history, processing status, and evidence for a previously returned work.

Use when: Verifying a claim, generating citations, explaining source coverage, or showing how a result was actually obtained.
Do NOT use when: You haven't retrieved/resolved anything about this work yet -- there's nothing to show evidence for.
Typically follows: Any of the other tools, once you have a canonical_id to ask about.
Typically followed by: (usually the last tool in a chain, feeding the final answer's citations)
Side effects: None -- pure read of what already happened.
tools.name: get_research_evidence
